Field surveys of captive colonies maintained at a baseline body temperature of 36.9 °C [T = 36.9 °C] have provided empirical estimates for several key life-history traits of the Western tree hyrax (Dendrohyrax dorsalis). Neonatal mass, recorded from a sample of thirty-two pups born across two breeding seasons, averaged 367 grams [Wwb = 367 grams], a value consistent with the moderate degree of precociality observed in this species. This initial birth weight, representing roughly seven percent of the adult female's body mass, is relatively high compared to many other small-bodied afrotherians. The gestation period underlying this investment, determined from observed copulation dates and subsequent parturition events, extends for approximately 213 days [tg = approximately 213 days] at the species' typical core temperat at a temperature of 36.9 °C [T = 36.9 °C]ure of 36.9 °C. This prolonged pregnancy, spanning over seven months, aligns with the slow life-history pace documented among hyraxes and other related taxa in the order Hyracoidea.

The weaning process marks a critical transition from maternal dependency to nutritional independence for the developing juvenile. Under controlled conditions maintained at 36.9 °C [T = 36.9 °C], lactation continues until the offspring reaches approximately 98 days since birth [tx = approximately 98 days since birth], meaning nutritional emancipation from the dam is typically achieved during the fourth month post-partum. This duration of maternal provisioning is comparatively lengthy for a mammal of this body size, reflecting the relatively slow developmental tempo characteristic of the species. Following weaning, the milk-dependent young must navigate a period of solid food transition during which they learn to identify palatable leaves, fruits, and bark items through observational learning from the mother and other colony members. The suckling juvenile stage is therefore extended, allowing ample time for the offspring to build the necessary gut flora and foraging skills required for independent survival in the forest canopy.

Sexual maturation in female Dendrohyrax dorsalis, as assessed through the onset of first estrus and the development of functional ovarian tissue, does not occur until approximately 488 days after birth [tp = approximately 488 days after birth] when individuals are housed at a constant ambient temperature of 36.9 °C [T = 36.9 °C]. This relatively delayed puberty, occurring more than sixteen months post-partum, represents a notable investment in somatic development before reproductive capability is attained. The extended juvenile and sub-adult period allows for the completion of skeletal growth and the accumulation of sufficient fat reserves that are likely critical for supporting the energetic demands of gestation and subsequent lactation. During this prolonged pre-reproductive phase, immature individuals exhibit considerable exploratory behavior and establish the social hierarchies that will define their adult breeding status within their arboreal territories.

Adult body size represents a fundamental constraint on the energetic budget of any mammalian species. The maximum recorded wet weight for adult Dendrohyrax dorsalis in field studies approaches 5000 grams [Wwi = 5000 grams], a figure that places this species among the larger members of the genus. This ultimate wet weight is attained after several years of gradual mass accumulation following the onset of sexual maturity, with individuals continuing to add skeletal and muscular tissue well into their social prime. The substantial adult mass, which is roughly thirteen times the weight at birth, requires a correspondingly high daily food intake to sustain metabolic demands, particularly given the relatively low nutritional quality of the folivorous diet this species consumes. Observations of marked individuals indicate that both males and females can achieve this mass, though males typically exhibit slightly heavier asymptotes, a pattern of dimorphism common among arboreal mammals living in multi-male groups.

Longevity estimates for this arboreal folivore, derived from mark-recapture studies of wild populations and comparative data from the closely related Cape hyrax (Procavia capensis), suggest a maximum lifespan of approximately 12 years [am = approximately 12 years] under natural conditions at the species' core body temperature of 36.9 °C [T = 36.9 °C]. This relatively extended lifespan, characteristic of hyraxes in general, allows for multiple reproductive opportunities over an individual's lifetime, though the annual reproductive output is correspondingly modest. Adult females typically produce a single litter of one to three pups each year [Ri = one to three pups each year], with an inter-birth interval exceeding twelve months [F_R_i = an inter-birth interval exceeding twelve months], a pattern consistent with the K-selected life-history strategy observed across the Hyracoidea.
